extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in number theory and the history/proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions, equivalent formulations, historical partial results, and the modern proof strategy (via elliptic curves and modularity) for Fermat's Last Theorem; useful for someone studying or explaining the theorem and its proof. Covers reductions, special-exponent proofs, key theorems (Kummer, Ribet, modularity) and computational verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Fermat's Last Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For any integer n > 2, the equation a^n + b^n = c^n has no positive integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central claim of the article; the cases n = 1 and n = 2 have infinitely many solutions and are excluded. The statement is presented as the theorem to be proved (historically a conjecture until Wiles's proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — trivial vs non-trivial solution
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution to x^n + y^n = z^n where one or more of x, y, or z is zero is a trivial solution. A solution where all three are nonzero is a non-trivial solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many equivalent formulations and reductions consider non-trivial solutions only; equivalence over N, Z and Q uses this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulations over N, Z, and Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent statement 1: x^n + y^n = z^n, n >= 3, has no non-trivial solutions x,y,z in Z. Equivalent statement 2: for integer n >= 3, no non-trivial solutions exist in Q. Equivalent statement 3: x^n + y^n = 1, n >= 3, has no non-trivial solutions x,y in Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains how these formulations are equivalent by sign changes, clearing denominators, or normalizing by z (to reduce to v^n + w^n = 1). This normalization is useful because it reduces a 3-variable surface problem to a 2-variable curve problem over Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to prime exponents (suffices to check n = 4 and odd primes)
rubrics_metrics.description: After handling n = 4, it suffices to prove the theorem for all odd prime exponents p, because if a solution exists for composite n = de then (a^d, b^d, c^d) is a solution for exponent e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fermat proved n = 4; the reduction argument shows only prime exponents (and n = 4) need separate proof, which focused subsequent work on prime exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frey curve construction (connection to elliptic curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a, b, c is a non-trivial solution to a^p + b^p = c^p (p an odd prime), then the Frey curve y^2 = x(x - a^p)(x + b^p) is an elliptic curve that (according to Frey's observation) would have unusual properties and be unlikely to be modular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction is the bridge linking Fermat's equation to the modularity problem; any purported counterexample yields a semistable elliptic curve with properties contradicting modularity, enabling a strategy to prove FLT by proving modularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity theorem requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The (Taniyama–Shimura–Weil) modularity theorem: every elliptic curve is modular (equivalently, can be associated with a unique modular form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving the modularity theorem (or at least for semistable elliptic curves) was the key step: together with Ribet's theorem (which links a Fermat counterexample to a non-modular Frey curve), modularity implies no counterexample can exist, therefore FLT holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ribet's theorem (the epsilon conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribet proved that the Frey curve constructed from a hypothetical solution to Fermat's equation would not be modular (this completed Serre's program relating such curves to modularity and is the missing link showing that modularity of semistable elliptic curves implies FLT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ribet's theorem is the crucial contrapositive step: it converts any putative Fermat counterexample into a semistable non-modular elliptic curve; therefore, proving modularity for such curves eliminates possible counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wiles's proof strategy and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles proved enough of the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves (using Galois representations, Iwasawa-type methods, Euler systems and deformation theory of Galois representations) to imply FLT when combined with Ribet's theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that Wiles's original large proof contained a flaw that was later fixed (with Richard Taylor) by proving ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras; publication in 1995 completed the proof. The proof required modern 20th-century techniques far beyond Fermat's era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite descent for n = 4
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's proof for the case n = 4 uses infinite descent to show that x^4 - y^4 = z^2 has no primitive integer solutions, which implies FLT for exponent 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the only surviving Fermat proof and serves as the classical reduction step that allows the general problem to be reduced to odd prime exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kummer's approach and the regular-prime criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Kummer proved FLT for all regular primes by developing the theory of 'ideal numbers' to handle the failure of unique factorization in cyclotomic fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular primes are those for which Kummer's methods (based on cyclotomic fields and class number conditions) succeed; irregular primes remained problematic and had to be addressed individually or by other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of unique factorization and ideal numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamé's attempted proof failed because it assumed unique factorization in cyclotomic fields; Kummer resolved this by inventing ideal numbers to restore a setting in which factorization arguments could work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical lesson explained is that algebraic structure (UFD vs failure of UFD) is a critical technical requirement for proofs that attempt to factor a^p + b^p in cyclotomic extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophie Germain's auxiliary primes / non-consecutivity condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Germain defined auxiliary primes θ = 2 h p + 1 and showed that if no integers raised to the pth power were adjacent modulo θ (the 'non-consecutivity condition'), then θ must divide the product xyz; she used this to prove the first case of FLT for many primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Her approach aimed to prove the first case (p not dividing xyz) for infinitely many primes or classes of primes; she proved results for odd primes less than certain bounds and for primes with auxiliary primes of particular primality properties (e.g., if 2p+1 is prime).

rubrics_metrics.name: First case vs second case of FLT
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'first case' of FLT: the prime p does not divide the product xyz of a putative solution; the 'second case' deals with when p divides one of the variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many partial results (Sophie Germain, Kummer, computational verifications) address the first case separately from the second case; proofs or criteria often distinguish these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational verification as partial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational methods have been used to verify FLT for all prime exponents up to large bounds (e.g., up to four million by 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While useful for checking many exponents, computational verification cannot prove the general theorem since an exponent beyond the checked bound could theoretically produce a counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mordell conjecture / Faltings' theorem implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Mordell conjectured (and Faltings later proved) that curves of genus > 1 over number fields have only finitely many rational points; this implies Fermat's equation for fixed n > 2 has at most finitely many primitive integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faltings' theorem provides a finiteness perspective on Diophantine equations of the type arising from normalization of FLT, although it does not by itself prove non-existence of any non-trivial solutions for all n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent statement via modularity contradiction (Equivalent statement 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent statement 4: if a, b, c is a non-trivial solution for an odd prime p, then the associated Frey curve y^2 = x(x - a^p)(x + b^p) will be an elliptic curve without a modular form; but Wiles's proof shows such curves must be modular, yielding a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates the core logical contrapositive: proving modularity for the relevant class of elliptic curves rules out any Fermat counterexample by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of many ad hoc and exponent-specific proofs historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, FLT was proved for many specific exponents (p = 3, 5, 7, 6, 10, 14, etc.) using various ad hoc infinite-descent or other arguments tied to individual exponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents these exponent-specific proofs to show the gradual progress and why a general proof required new, deeper concepts rather than extension of ad hoc methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criterion — modern proof needs new global techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The eventual successful strategy required linking different areas (elliptic curves, modular forms, Galois representations, deformation theory) rather than purely elementary descent or factorization methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that Wiles's and collaborators' techniques were 20th-century developments, illustrating that the problem's solution required broad, modern machinery; this is a criterion for what constitutes a complete modern proof.
